events.title: Fortran 2003 standardized
events.summary: On November 18, 2004, the Fortran 2003 standard was published — adding object-oriented features and direct calls to C libraries.
events.about: Fortran 2003 let scientific code use objects (like classes in other languages) and call C libraries directly — critical for linking with modern GPU tools and numerical packages without awkward glue code. Mixed Fortran/C/C++ supercomputing projects became much simpler.

narrative.whyChosen: Fortran 2003 brought object-oriented design and C interoperability — what HPC teams needed to integrate with the rest of the software world.
narrative.whyImportant: Direct C linking and improved memory handling made Fortran viable alongside C and C++ in large supercomputing projects.
narrative.problemSolved: Fortran 95 couldn't cleanly talk to C libraries or express object-oriented models that researchers expected from other languages.

events.title: Firefox 1.0 released
events.summary: The Mozilla Foundation shipped Firefox 1.0 on November 9, 2004 — a fast, tabbed, extension-friendly browser that broke Internet Explorer's monopoly.
events.about: Firefox grew from the Phoenix/Firebird project as the lean alternative to the bloated Mozilla Suite. Extensions (Adblock, Greasemonkey), tabbed browsing, and aggressive standards support made it the browser developers recommended — and proved the web did not have to be IE-only.

narrative.whyChosen: Firefox 1.0 was the first credible open-source challenger to IE's market dominance.
narrative.whyImportant: It revived competition, pushed web standards, and inspired the extension ecosystem.
narrative.problemSolved: Users and developers were stuck on IE 6 with no secure, modern alternative backed by a major open project.
